title: Writing tips: Build a Sentence, email and discussion templates
lines: The Writing section has 12 items in 23 minutes: ten Build a Sentence items, one Write an Email task and one Write for an Academic Discussion task. Each needs a different skill, so practice them separately and then together under time.
## Build a Sentence
You see a short exchange and a reply made of word chunks in the wrong order. You put the chunks in order to make one correct, natural sentence. Some items include an extra chunk that does not belong.
- Read the first line of the exchange. The reply must answer it.
- Find the subject and main verb first, then build around them.

- Check question order: in a direct question the auxiliary comes before the subject ("Did you finish..."); in an indirect question the subject comes before the verb ("Do you know where the office is?").
- Place adverbs of frequency before the main verb and after "be": "She usually arrives early", "He is always on time".
- Look for fixed patterns: "not only ... but also", "so ... that", "the reason why", relative clauses with who, which and that.
- If there is an extra chunk, it is often a duplicate preposition, a wrong auxiliary (does instead of did) or a wrong word form.
> Exchange: "Where should I submit the form?" Chunks: [the office] [you can] [it at] [leave] [on the second floor]
> Answer: You can leave it at the office on the second floor.
! Read your finished sentence silently from start to end. If it sounds wrong in your head, it probably is.
## Write an Email (7 minutes)

You read a situation and three points you must cover. The reader might be a professor, a manager, a landlord or a customer service team. You are scored on how clearly and politely you complete the task and on your language.
- Cover all three points. Missing one is the most expensive mistake.
- Match the tone to the reader: polite and formal for a professor, friendly but clear for a classmate.
- Give specific details. "The heater in my room has not worked since Monday" is better than "There is a problem".
- In our experience, a good email in 7 minutes is usually about 120 to 180 words. Quality and completeness matter more than length.
Template (adapt it, do not copy it word for word in every email):
> Dear Professor Chen,
> I am writing about [reason]. [One or two sentences of context.]
> [Point 1: explain the problem or situation with a detail.]
> [Point 2: make your request politely. "Would it be possible to...?" "I would be grateful if you could..."]
> [Point 3: suggest a solution or give extra details. "If that is not possible, I could..."]
> Thank you for your time and help. I look forward to hearing from you.
> Best regards,
> Priya
Useful phrases:
- Explaining: "Unfortunately, ...", "The reason I am writing is that...", "I have noticed that..."
- Requesting: "Would it be possible to...?", "Could you let me know whether...?", "I would appreciate it if..."
- Suggesting: "One option might be to...", "Perhaps we could...", "I would be happy to..."
- Closing: "Thank you in advance.", "Please let me know if you need any further information."
! Do not start every sentence with "I". Vary your openings: "Unfortunately", "Because of this", "If possible", "In addition".
## Write for an Academic Discussion (10 minutes)
A professor posts a question to an online class. Two students reply with different views. You write your own contribution.
- Read the professor's question carefully. What exactly is being asked?
- Choose a position quickly. Pick the side you can support best, not the side you think is "correct".
- Add something new. Do not just repeat what the students said. Give a new reason or a new example.
- Refer to at least one student by name to show you are taking part in the discussion.
- An effective response is usually at least 100 words. Aim for about 120 to 150 well-organized words.
Template:
> [Position] In my view, ... / I believe ... because ...
> [Link to a student] Mateo makes a good point about ..., but I think he overlooks ... / I agree with Aisha that ..., and I would add that ...
> [New reason] The main reason is that ...
> [Example] For example, in my own city / at my school / in a study I read about, ...
> [Closing] For these reasons, I think ...
> Example contribution (topic: should universities require first-year students to live on campus?):

> I believe first-year students should be encouraged, but not required, to live on campus. Sofia argues that dormitory life helps new students make friends, and that is true for many people. However, I think she overlooks the cost. For some families, a dormitory is much more expensive than living at home, and a rule like this could stop talented students from enrolling. A better approach would be to offer social events and study groups for students who commute, so they can build friendships too. For example, my cousin's college runs evening clubs for commuters, and they are always full. For these reasons, a flexible policy seems fairer.
## Checking your writing in the last minute
- Did you answer every part of the task?
- Verb tenses and subject-verb agreement (he has, they have).
- Articles (a, an, the) and plurals.
- Spelling of key words from the prompt. Copy them correctly.
- One idea per sentence. Split very long sentences.
## Practice routine
- Build a Sentence: one set of 10 a day for a week, timed. Note the grammar point of each mistake.
- Email: three emails a week, then compare with the model and the checklist.
- Discussion: three posts a week. Before writing, list two possible new reasons in 30 seconds. This trains fast planning.
